title: Iterator Pattern
oneLiner: Walks through a collection one item at a time, without the caller ever needing to know how that collection is actually stored.

hero.name: Wayfinder
hero.catchphrase: One step at a time — you don't need to know the map.
hero.power: Traverses any collection uniformly, hiding whether it's an array, tree, or linked list underneath.
hero.weakness: If the underlying collection changes shape mid-traversal, Wayfinder can lose its place — classic 'concurrent modification' bugs.
hero.origin: Wayfinder appeared after a reporting tool had one loop for arrays, another for linked lists, and a third for trees — three copies of the exact same reporting logic.

story.problem: A reporting function has one code path for arrays (`for (let i = 0; ...)`), another for a custom linked list (`while (node) { node = node.next }`), and a third for a tree. Every report duplicates all three.
story.solution: Wayfinder gives every collection the same `Iterator` interface — `hasNext()` and `next()`. The reporting function loops over any of them identically.
story.result: One reporting loop works across arrays, linked lists, and trees. Each collection knows how to traverse itself; the caller never needs to.

before: One traversal implementation per collection type
Callers need to know each collection's internal structure
after: One uniform hasNext()/next() interface for every collection
Callers never touch a collection's internal structure

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: Three nearly-identical report functions sit side by side: one for arrays, one for linked lists, one for trees.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: I just fixed a bug in the array report and now I have to remember to fix the exact same bug in two other copies.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: Wayfinder appears holding a compass that works identically no matter the terrain.
panels.speaker: Wayfinder
panels.dialogue: You don't need three maps. Give every collection the same way to walk through it — hasNext(), next(). I'll handle the terrain.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: Array, LinkedList, and Tree each implement the same Iterator interface, hiding their internal structure.
panels.speaker: Wayfinder
panels.dialogue: Write your report loop once, against the interface. It works identically whether it's walking an array or a tree.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: The three duplicate report functions collapse into one, working across every collection type.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: One report function now. One bug fix location. And it works on any collection we add in the future too.

useWhen: You need to traverse different kinds of collections through one uniform interface.
You want to hide a collection's internal structure (array, tree, linked list) from the code that processes its elements.
You need multiple independent traversals over the same collection at once.
avoidWhen: Your language already provides a built-in, idiomatic iteration protocol (like JS's `for...of` / `Symbol.iterator`) — reinventing it adds nothing.
There's only ever one collection type and no real duplication to eliminate.
The collection is small and simple enough that direct indexing is clearer than a custom iterator.
commonMistakes: Building a custom Iterator interface when the language's native iteration protocol already solves the problem.
Not handling concurrent modification — mutating a collection while an iterator is mid-traversal, causing skipped or duplicated elements.
Exposing internal collection details through the iterator anyway, defeating the point of the abstraction.
Forgetting that some traversal orders (in-order vs. pre-order for a tree) need their own dedicated iterator implementation.
explanation.realWorldExample: JavaScript's own iteration protocol (`Symbol.iterator`, `for...of`), Java's `Iterator`/`Iterable` interfaces, and database cursors that stream rows one at a time without loading the whole result set into memory are all Iterator.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: Doesn't every modern language already have iteration built in?

conversation.speaker: Wayfinder
conversation.message: Usually, yes — and you should use that first. I matter most for custom or unusual data structures the language's built-in loops don't already understand, like a tree or a paginated remote dataset.

conversation.speaker: Wayfinder
conversation.message: If the collection changes shape while I'm mid-walk through it — an item removed, a node added — I can lose my place or skip elements entirely.

codeBattle.scenario: Your app has a custom Tree data structure and needs to support both depth-first and breadth-first traversal for different reporting features, without those reports knowing the tree's internal shape.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: Wayfinder lets you build two different traversal-order iterators (depth-first, breadth-first) behind the same hasNext()/next() interface, so reports never touch the tree's internal structure.

quiz.question: What does Iterator hide from the code that processes a collection's elements?
options: The collection's internal structure (array, tree, linked list, etc.)
The values of the elements themselves
Whether the collection is empty or not
quiz.answer: The collection's internal structure (array, tree, linked list, etc.)
quiz.explanation: Iterator's whole value is letting callers traverse without caring how the data is actually stored.

quiz.question: What two methods typically define a basic Iterator interface?
quiz.explanation: These two methods are enough to walk through any sequence, one element at a time, regardless of underlying structure.

quiz.question: When should you avoid building a custom Iterator?
options: When your language's built-in iteration protocol already solves the same problem
When you have a custom tree structure with no native traversal support
When you need multiple independent traversals of the same collection
When you want to hide a complex data structure's internals
quiz.answer: When your language's built-in iteration protocol already solves the same problem
quiz.explanation: Reimplementing what `for...of` or `Iterable` already does adds needless complexity.

quiz.question: What bug class is Iterator particularly vulnerable to?
options: Concurrent modification — the collection changing shape while iteration is in progress
Memory leaks from unclosed file handles
Race conditions between two separate threads reading immutable data
quiz.answer: Concurrent modification — the collection changing shape while iteration is in progress
quiz.explanation: If the underlying collection is mutated mid-traversal, the iterator's position can become invalid or skip/duplicate elements.
